Screech
SKREECH
n. / adj. (a harsh cry; in the AV, the screech owl that shall rest in the ruins of Edom)
Imitative, from Middle English scrichen. At Isaiah 34:14 screech owl renders Hebrew lilith, a night creature — a bird of the waste places that finds a rest where a nation stood.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah 34 is the burden against Edom, and its judgment is described entirely by who moves in afterward: The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; the screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest. The verses around it fill out the inventory — thorns in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses, an habitation of dragons and a court for owls, the cormorant and the bittern in possession, the line of confusion and the stones of emptiness stretched over the whole.

The phrase that carries the horror is the quietest one: the night bird shall find for herself a place of rest. Where a kingdom was, something now roosts comfortably. Scripture uses this picture more than once — Isaiah 13 does the same to Babylon, and Job in his misery says I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls, meaning that he now keeps the company of the ruins. The theological point is not ornithological. The desolate places in the prophets are always the consequence of a specific judgment on a specific pride, and the creatures are there to show that the judgment was total: not a city with fewer people, but a city with none, and a bird asleep in the palace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a harsh, shrill cry; the cry of an owl in the night.

expand to see more

SCREECH, v.i. To cry out with a sharp shrill voice; to utter a sudden, sharp outcry, as in terror.

SCREECH-OWL, n. An owl whose scream is considered a bad omen; a bird of the night.

DESOLATE, a. Destitute of inhabitants; deserted; uninhabited; laid waste; in a ruinous condition.

BITTERN, n. A fowl of the grallic order, frequenting fens and marshes, noted for a booming cry.

CORMORANT, n. A large water fowl of the pelican kind, remarkable for its voracity.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 34:14 — "The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; the screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest."

Isaiah 34:13 — "And thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof: and it shall be an habitation of dragons, and a court for owls."

Isaiah 34:11 — "But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness."

Isaiah 13:21 — "But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there."

Modern Corruption

The prophetic ruin-scenes are treated as poetry with no historical reference, when the cities named were real, the judgments fell, and the sites can still be walked.

expand to see more

Isaiah 34 and Isaiah 13 name specific nations — Edom, Babylon — and predict specific ends. The habit of reading these chapters as generalized poetic imagery about divine displeasure empties them of exactly what the prophets meant them to carry: a testable claim. Edom is gone. Babylon is a ruin field. The Reformed handling of prophecy has always insisted that the prophets spoke to real history and that history answered, which is why the confessions treat fulfilled prophecy as an evidence of Scripture's divine authorship rather than as a literary feature.

The other temptation is to turn the beast-lists into a bestiary and argue about whether lilith is an owl, a night-hag or a demon. The Hebrew is genuinely obscure and the AV made a reasonable choice; nothing in the doctrine hangs on the species. What the passage means is unmistakable whichever creature it is: the palaces have thorns in them, the fortresses have brambles, and a night bird has found a comfortable roost where a nation used to be. That is what the end of a proud people looks like from the outside, and the prophets describe it so that other proud peoples might hear it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lilith (H3917), a night creature; tsiyyim (H6728), desert beasts; shamamah (H8077), desolation.

expand to see more

Hebrew lilith (H3917) — a creature of the night; rendered screech owl, used once in Scripture.

Hebrew tsiyyim (H6728) — dwellers in the dry places; the wild beasts of the desert.

Hebrew qav tohu (H6957, H8414) — the line of confusion; the surveyor's cord of emptiness stretched over Edom.

Hebrew shamamah (H8077) — desolation, waste; the standing prophetic term for a judged land.

Hebrew tannim (H8577) — dragons or jackals; the habitation of the ruined palaces.

Usage

"“the screech owl also shall rest there” — something roosting where a kingdom stood."

"“thorns shall come up in her palaces” — the inventory of a total judgment."

"“the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness” — a surveyor's cord over nothing."
